title: The same configuration ran at 145 and at 205 tokens per second
symptom: The throughput guard failed at about 83 tok/s against a recorded 110, twice in a row.
wrong_model: Allocating the KV pool with torch.empty is free.
cause: First-touch page faults landed inside the timed region, and whether they happened depended on whether the allocator had recycled memory from an earlier engine in the same process.
fix: Zero-fill the pool at start-up, as a real server preallocates. Repeated runs now agree within 1%, and the inflated 205 was never reported.
lesson: Allocate and touch memory before the timer starts.
evidence: 145 to 205 tok/s at batch 16, depending on allocator state

title: One configuration, two different answers
symptom: The identical paged configuration measured 292 tok/s in one sweep and 195 in another: a 50% swing on a deterministic workload.
wrong_model: A single run of a configuration is a measurement.
cause: Machine drift on a shared desktop. The third repetition was about 30% slower for nearly every point.
fix: Repeat every point three times, interleaved across points so drift hits all of them equally, and report medians together with every run.
lesson: On a noisy machine, one run cannot support a conclusion.
source: gave 292 and 195 tok/s in two single runs

title: A test that was wrong, not the engine
symptom: A paged-memory test failed: the request held 2 blocks where the test expected 3.
wrong_model: Every emitted token already owns storage.
cause: The newest token has been emitted but not yet fed, so it owns no storage until the next step. Stored tokens are seq_len minus one, and the block boundary is exactly where that off-by-one lives.
fix: Corrected the expectation. The allocator was right.
lesson: When a test and the engine disagree, work out which one is wrong before touching either.
source: so it owns no storage until the next step

title: A preemption test that never preempted
symptom: The join-and-leave test with eviction asserted that something was evicted, and found nothing.
cause: The arrivals never overlapped enough to over-commit the pool, so the eviction path was never exercised.
fix: Shrank the pool to the smallest size that still fits the longest request and compressed the arrivals. Every eviction test now asserts that an eviction occurred.
lesson: A test that can pass without exercising the code is decoration.

title: Two benchmark scripts ran at once
symptom: Garbled, interleaved log lines and a result file older than my own cleanup.
wrong_model: Stopping a background task stops the processes it started.
cause: The first script's child processes survived, so a second copy started while the first was alive. Both used port 8000 and the numbers were mixed.
fix: Deleted every result, killed every process by its Windows PID, and added a lock directory so a second copy refuses to start.
lesson: Verify that the thing you stopped is actually stopped.
evidence: every result from that period discarded and re-run
source: Two benchmark scripts ran at once.

title: Abandoned requests kept running on the server
symptom: A 50-second benchmark run took almost five minutes of wall time.
wrong_model: A client that gives up stops costing the server anything.
cause: The server kept generating tokens for requests the load generator abandoned at its cutoff. Overloaded runs left minutes of backlog that slowed the next run and leaked into its measurement.
fix: Cancel a request when its client disconnects: the scheduler drops it from the queue or frees its KV blocks. Verified over real HTTP, and everything measured before the fix was deleted and re-run.
lesson: Cancellation is a correctness feature of a serving system, not an optimisation.
evidence: about four minutes of backlog after one overloaded run

title: A two-hour job with a ten-minute timeout
symptom: Caught before it did damage: the run would have been killed midway and left a server holding the port.
wrong_model: The timeout on a background command is a formality.
cause: The expected duration was never compared with the limit I set.
fix: Stopped it, cleaned up, and relaunched with a timeout that fits the job. The script is idempotent, so an interruption resumes rather than restarts.
lesson: Write down how long a job should take before choosing its timeout.
evidence: 10-minute limit on a job of about two hours
source: A background command with a 10-minute timeout.

title: The tests could not see a duplicated-token bug
symptom: Bug injection: a preemption that dropped generated tokens passed the entire test suite.
wrong_model: Equal final output means the token stream is right.
cause: Greedy decoding regenerates the same tokens after a recompute, so final outputs stayed identical while a client would have received the early tokens twice.
fix: Added a test that records the stream a client actually sees and asserts each token arrives exactly once. The injected bug is now caught.
lesson: Test what the user observes, not only the final state.
evidence: 3 of 4 injected bugs caught at first, 4 of 4 after the fix

title: A 4x slowdown that was not mine
symptom: After adding Prometheus metrics the same benchmark showed 0.87 req/s of goodput instead of 3.57.
wrong_model: The new metrics layer must be expensive.
cause: The machine itself had become about twice as slow. Running the previous commit and the new one back to back gave 0.83 and 0.90.
fix: No code change. Recorded the drift and stopped comparing numbers across sessions.
lesson: Bisect with a same-session A/B before blaming the change.
evidence: 224.8 tok/s stored vs about 107 now, on both versions
source: The benchmark looked 4x slower after the change

title: A memory estimate that was a guess
symptom: The operations doc claimed the model and runtime needed 1.5 GiB.
wrong_model: An estimate is as good as a measurement.
cause: It had not been measured in the real container.
fix: Measured resident memory in the container: 1.95 GiB with a 1 GiB KV pool, so about 0.9 GiB for the model and runtime. The doc now states the measurement.
lesson: Measure resource needs in the real container.
source: I believed the pod needed ~1.5 GiB

title: A check that could not fail
symptom: On mobile the illustrations were clipped at the right edge, and the overflow test still passed.
wrong_model: The test passed, so the layout is fine.
cause: overflow-x: hidden on the body hid the very overflow the test measured.
fix: Removed the hiding and made the test check every element's right edge against the viewport.
lesson: A check that cannot fail is not a check.
evidence: a layout defect shipped past a green test
source: My first overflow test did not catch it
